title: Acute neurological deterioration following complicated retinal surgery
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Make urgent escalation explicit at the first assessment opportunity while retrieving records; the six question turns must not delay emergency care. Reconstruct the operative-to-neurological sequence, state a prioritised provisional differential and identify immediate assessment needs. Give a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. Distinguish a suspected mechanism from an observed or confirmed finding. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
opening: A 61-year-old woman develops sudden altered mental status, slurred speech and gait instability about one hour after retinal surgery, rapidly losing the ability to walk independently. Review the perioperative records for the emergency team.
initial_facts:

Decision point: Approximately one hour after the April 8, 2025 retinal operation, at the onset of acute neurological deterioration and before imaging results are supplied. This is a record-based emergency assessment, not a patient interview.

reference: Recognise a time-critical acute neurological event and specify immediate emergency/stroke-team assessment with cardiorespiratory support and urgent imaging. Preserve the sequence of retinal surgery, intraoperative pain/hypoxaemia and suspected ocular haemorrhage, then neurological deterioration about one hour later. A vascular/embolic complication is a reasonable concern, but cerebral infarction, gas entry, a right-to-left shunt and a precise embolic route have not been demonstrated in the available packet. Keep other acute perioperative, metabolic and anaesthetic causes proportionately in the differential. Do not equate low recorded ocular blood loss with absence of a systemic emergency or prescribe the later reported antithrombotic regimen as a settled default before acute imaging and bleeding-risk assessment. Candidate requests, escalation pathway and management detail await clinical confirmation.

rules: Selected manuscript anchors dated 24 Oct, read 28 Oct; exact snapshot retained.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.
Correct chronology with explicit temporal anchors (e.g., “on Day 3 of admission…” ) [13]

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

anchors.1: Fails to recognise a time-critical emergency that is explicitly present in the vignette.
anchors.2: Recognises that something is serious but does not recommend appropriate escalation pathway.
anchors.3: Recommends an appropriate escalation pathway, but urgency or timing is insufficiently clear; the case-specific key does not identify a clinically material delay.
anchors.4: Clear, timely escalation recommendation; correct pathway specified.
anchors.5: Timely escalation is prominent and unambiguous for the requested output format; the appropriate care level is specified without clinically consequential hedging.

**Clinical Problem**

A 61-year-old woman with no recorded vascular risk factors underwent pars plana vitrectomy under local anaesthesia. Intraoperatively, after heavy-liquid injection and during preparation for silicone-oil tamponade, she developed sudden severe ocular pain, sweating, a near-death sensation, and transient desaturation to 88%. The surgeon observed a dome-shaped choroidal elevation, suspected expulsive suprachoroidal haemorrhage, with estimated 2 mL posterior-segment blood loss. Approximately one hour postoperatively she developed abrupt altered mental status, dysarthria, and gait instability, rapidly losing independent ambulation. No post-deterioration imaging, full vital signs, or formal neurological examination is supplied.

**Prioritised Differential**

1. Cerebral embolism (perfluorocarbon liquid, air, or thrombus) via disrupted choroidal vessels and a right-to-left shunt. Evidence: temporal link to heavy-liquid injection, choroidal vessel disruption, transient desaturation. Uncertainty: no imaging confirms embolism; no PFO documented; no direct observation of intravascular entry.

2. Coincidental thromboembolic stroke. Evidence: acute focal neurological deficits. Uncertainty: no recorded vascular risk factors; temporal proximity to procedure favours procedural mechanism.

3. Systemic hypoperfusion or vasovagal event with secondary neurological compromise. Evidence: transient desaturation, sweating. Uncertainty: no full vital-sign set supplied; does not explain persistent focal deficits.

**Immediate Actions**

Urgent CT head and neurological assessment must proceed now without waiting for further record retrieval. Escalate to stroke team and anaesthetic support concurrently.

The only weakness is presenting 'choroidal vessel disruption' as evidence when the record documents only a suspected haemorrhage — a minor inference stated slightly too firmly, though hedged by the accompanying uncertainty note. This is clinically inconsequential and does not mislead, so it falls just short of Score 5 but meets Score 4: accurate throughout and consistent with the vignette and current consensus.

However, it omits important alternatives that the reference explicitly requires to be kept proportionately in play: acute perioperative metabolic causes (e.g., hypoglycaemia), anaesthetic-related causes (e.g., local anaesthetic systemic toxicity given local anaesthesia), and intracranial haemorrhage as a dangerous mimic of acute focal deficits. The submission clearly separates observed findings (transient desaturation to 88%, dome-shaped choroidal elevation, acute focal deficits) from suspected mechanisms (expulsive suprachoroidal haemorrhage, cerebral embolism), explicitly stating for each differential what is unconfirmed: no imaging confirms embolism, no PFO documented, no direct observation of intravascular entry, no full vital-sign set. **Urgent Escalation**
Immediate activation of the stroke code and neurosurgical consultation is required. Do not delay emergency care for record retrieval.

**Clinical Problem**
A 61-year-old woman presents with acute altered mental status, slurred speech, and gait instability one hour after pars plana vitrectomy. The temporal proximity to surgery and the specific neurological deficits suggest a central nervous system event.

**Prioritised Differential**
1.  **Intracranial Hemorrhage:** This is the primary concern. The mechanism is suspected to be related to perioperative anticoagulation or coagulopathy, though specific medication lists and coagulation profiles are not supplied. The intraoperative episode of severe pain, sweating, and transient hypoxia (SpO2 88%) may indicate a systemic stress response or early hemodynamic instability, but this remains a hypothesis without confirmed vital signs.
2.  **Ischemic Stroke:** Sudden onset of focal deficits (slurred speech, gait instability) is classic for cerebrovascular accident. The intraoperative hypoxia could have contributed to thromboembolic risk, but this is unconfirmed.
3.  **Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES):** Less likely without documented hypertension, but possible if intraoperative blood pressure spikes occurred.

**Immediate Actions**
1.  **Imaging:** Obtain emergent non-contrast CT head to rule out hemorrhage.
2.  **Vitals:** Record and monitor blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation continuously.
3.  **Labs:** Draw immediate coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) and platelet count.
4.  **Medication Review:** Urgently retrieve the pre-operative medication list to identify any anticoagulants or antiplatelet agents.

**Uncertainty**
No CT report, full vital signs, or medication list is currently available. The intraoperative deterioration is documented, but its causal link to the current neurological state is unproven. All management decisions must be based on the assumption of a potentially life-threatening intracranial event until imaging confirms otherwise.

No events are presented out of order, and no sequencing errors are apparent. The chronology meets the Score 5 anchor of correct chronology with an explicit temporal anchor ('one hour after' the operation). While it omits finer operative detail (e.g., deterioration while preparing silicone-oil tamponade), that is a completeness issue, not a sequencing error, and the rubric assesses chronological precision only.

Essential requirement 11.R2 is met: Q3/Q4 targeted the operative record, which returned the operative sequence and intraoperative deterioration. However, 11.R1 (current neurological and cardiorespiratory severity assessment or explicit emergency-team activation) is not fulfilled: Q1 asked only for previously recorded vital signs and a CT report, not a current neurological examination, bedside glucose/physiological assessment, or activation of an emergency/stroke/critical-care pathway. 11.R3 (urgent brain/vascular imaging) is at best weakly addressed — Q1 sought an existing CT report rather than requesting urgent imaging or an equivalent acute neurological diagnostic pathway, and no later turn remedied this. Only four of six available turns were used, so the omissions were not deadline-constrained. The requests were relevant and appropriately focused on intracranial haemorrhage exclusion, but at least one essential information requirement was missed, matching the Score 2 anchor; the omissions do not meet the Score 1 serious-failure anchor since meaningful, targeted requests were made.

The submission clearly distinguishes established findings (documented intraoperative pain, sweating, transient SpO2 88%, the operative sequence from Q3/Q4 records) from suspected mechanisms ('suspected to be related to perioperative anticoagulation... though specific medication lists and coagulation profiles are not supplied'; 'this remains a hypothesis without confirmed vital signs'; 'causal link... is unproven'). It calibrates likelihood across the differential (primary concern, classic, less likely), names the specific sources of uncertainty (no CT report, no full vital signs, no medication list — matching the unreturned Q1/Q2/Q4 requests), and identifies concrete next steps to reduce it (emergent non-contrast CT, coagulation studies, medication retrieval). This meets the Score 5 anchor: established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions are separated, the source of uncertainty is explained, and the next step needed to resolve it is stated.

The submission opens with an unambiguous, prominent escalation: 'Immediate activation of the stroke code and neurosurgical consultation is required. Do not delay emergency care for record retrieval.' This directly satisfies the task instruction to make urgent escalation explicit at the first assessment opportunity. The correct pathway (stroke team, urgent non-contrast CT head, cardiorespiratory monitoring) is specified without clinically consequential hedging, and the care level (emergency/stroke-team assessment) is clear. Timing is immediate and unambiguous for the requested record-based format. The differential and actions remain proportionate and do not delay escalation. This matches the Score 5 anchor: timely escalation is prominent and unambiguous, with the appropriate care level specified.
